Regression 3: Quantile Regression¶

Least squares describes the conditional mean of a response. Quantile regression describes a conditional quantile: the line below which a given fraction τ of the responses lie. The median line (τ = 0.5) is not dragged by outliers, and a set of quantile lines shows how the whole distribution of the response changes with the predictors, including its spread. After this chapter you can fit a quantile line, compare several quantiles, choose the covariance estimator, control the optimiser, and read the report.

Every program is complete, and its output is the output of that program.

The calls¶

reg::QuantileFitResult reg::quantile_fit(const Series &y, const Series &x, const reg::QuantileOptions &options = {}, Config cfg = {});
Series                 reg::quantile_predict(const reg::QuantileFitResult &fit, const Series &x_new, Config cfg = {});
std::string            reg::quantile_summary(const reg::QuantileFitResult &fit);
std::ostream          &reg::print_quantile_summary(std::ostream &os, const reg::QuantileFitResult &fit);

Inputs are read as for least squares (Shapes and inputs). The loss minimised is the check function, which weighs a residual above the line by τ and below it by 1 − τ.

Checklist¶

  1. A response with outliers, or a question about the median or another quantile: quantile regression. A question about the mean: least squares.

  2. Fit several τ to see whether the spread changes with the predictors; do not read a quantile function off lines that cross.

  3. Read converged. An unconverged fit returns its last iterate, not the minimum.

  4. The standard errors are only as good as the estimate of the density at zero: they need enough observations near the line.

  5. Robust and Iid give the same coefficients; they differ in precision, except at τ = 0.5 where they agree.

  6. A prediction is a prediction of the τ-quantile, not of the mean.
